sessions: Hello, nice to meet you. My name is Yuki Tanabe. I am a freelance translator, Japanese to English mostly, sometimes English to Japanese. I live in Osaka, in Kita-ku, near Tenma, with my cat Mochi. My English is good for work but in casual writing sometimes strange, please forgive me.

First, a small question for warming up. How would you translate 「もったいない」 in a literary text? Not a business text. Every dictionary says "wasteful" but it feels too cold. The context is an old woman looking at a half-eaten persimmon her grandson left on the table.

Ah, I like your idea that sometimes we should not translate the word itself but the feeling around it. "She couldn't bear to see it go to waste" or even showing her picking it up and finishing it herself. The action can carry the word. Yes.

Some information about me, maybe useful later. I work best in the morning, from about 6 until lunch. Please never suggest calls or meetings after 9pm Japan time, I am finished by then, my brain becomes tofu. Many of my clients are in Europe so this is always a negotiation.
Also I have an allergy to buckwheat, quite serious. So no soba, and careful with some galettes and some Japanese sweets. If you suggest recipes or restaurants, please remember.

Now big news for me. A London publisher, Harbor Lane Press, offered me to translate a novel. It is 『塩の果樹園』 by Kawabe Rin, in English "The Salt Orchard". It is a quiet novel about a family running a mikan orchard in Wakayama near the sea, three generations, and the youngest daughter comes back from Tokyo. I love this book. It is my first full literary novel. Until now I did short stories and a lot of commercial work.
The editor at Harbor Lane is Thomas Pryce. He found me through a short story translation I did for a literary magazine. He is very kind, writes long emails with many semicolons.

The contract is not finished yet. They sent the terms and I agreed, but their legal team must prepare it and countersign. Until the contract is signed I don't want to start properly. Is that too careful?
Yes, I think so too. I will do some light reading and glossary preparation but not the real translation until it is signed. Thank you.
Can I ask about rates? For literary translation into English in the UK, what is a normal rate? They offered per 1,000 words. I want to know if it is fair before I sign.
Okay, so the Society of Authors gives guidance and what they offered is in the normal range, not high but fair for a first novel. Good, I feel better.
Last small thing: my cat Mochi has started to sleep on my keyboard every morning at exactly 6:30. Is there a scientific reason? She is ruining my best working hour.
Ha, warmth and attention. I will put a heated pad next to the laptop. Mochi, you win again. Thank you, see you next time.

Hello again. Today family topic. My younger sister Aoi is getting married! I am so happy. Her fiancé is Daniel Weber, he is German, works as an engineer in Kobe. They met at a climbing gym. He is very tall and very polite and he is learning Japanese very hard.

The wedding will be in Kyoto, at Kamogawa Garden Hall, near the river. The date is 11 April next year. Aoi asked me to give a speech at the reception, in Japanese and English both, because Daniel's family is coming from Hamburg.

I am nervous. I translate other people's words all day but my own words in front of 80 people, that is different. Can you give me some advice about structure of a bilingual wedding speech? Should I say everything twice?

Ah, I see, not everything twice, it becomes too long. Better to alternate: one part in Japanese, the next part in English, with small summary. And the most important line maybe in both. That is clever.
What are typical things not to say in a Japanese wedding speech? I know there are 忌み言葉 like "cut" or "separate" or "return". Can you list more so I can avoid them in both languages?
Oh, I forgot about repeated words like 「重ね重ね」 or 「たびたび」, because they suggest remarriage. In English I don't need to worry, but in the Japanese part, yes. Thank you.

Also Aoi wants me to help her choose a kimono for the 前撮り photo, the photo before the wedding. She is choosing between a white shiromuku and a colourful iro-uchikake. I don't have opinion, I just want her happy. What is the difference in meaning?
Interesting, the white means she is ready to be "dyed" in the colour of the new family, and the colourful one was for after the ceremony traditionally. Daniel will like this story. I will tell him.

And one more: Daniel asked me how to say "thank you for raising such a wonderful daughter" to my parents in Japanese, in a natural way, not like a textbook. Can you help? He wants to say it at the reception.
「素敵な娘さんを育ててくださって、本当にありがとうございます」 is good. Maybe I will teach him to bow a little at the end. He will practise in front of the mirror, he is that type.
Thank you! I feel a little more ready.

Hello. Today work. Harbor Lane still did not send the countersigned contract, but Thomas said to send him a sample of the first pages anyway so he can see my voice. Not official translation, just a sample. I think this is ok.

Here is my draft of the opening paragraphs. Please do not rewrite, but tell me where the rhythm feels "translated" and not natural English:

"The sea was visible from every row of the orchard, though no one in the Mizuno family ever looked at it. It was simply there, the way the sky was there, the way Grandmother's cough was there in the mornings, a fact of the place rather than a view. The trees grew in terraces up the hillside, each terrace held by a stone wall that had been built by hands no one living could name, and in winter the mikan hung among the dark leaves like small lamps someone had forgotten to put out.

Haruka came back in the second week of December, when the harvest was half finished and everyone was too tired to ask her why. She arrived on the last bus from Gobo, carrying one suitcase and a paper bag of Tokyo sweets that nobody would eat, because they were too sweet and too small and because they were from Tokyo. Her father met her at the bus stop with the light truck. He did not get out. He leaned across and opened the passenger door from inside, and the smell of the truck, oil and fruit and his cigarettes, which he had promised to stop, reached her before his voice did.

'You're thin,' he said.

'You're still smoking,' she said.

They drove up the hill without speaking further. Below them, the sea did what it always did, and neither of them looked at it."

Thank you. So, mostly it flows, but "a fact of the place rather than a view" maybe a little too clever, and "small lamps someone had forgotten to put out" is good but "forgotten" maybe should be "forgotten to turn off"? Hmm, no, "put out" is better for old lamps with flame. I keep it.

And you think "because they were from Tokyo" at the end of the list is good because the original also has this little joke? Yes, the original is 「東京のものだったから」, it is a small bitter joke. I am glad it survives.

Thomas also asked about the schedule. I told him I can deliver the first half, chapters 1 to 12, by 5 November, and the full draft at the end of January. He said that works for their plan to publish in spring 2028.
Spring 2028 seems so far! Is it normal that publishing is so slow? Two years after translation?
I see, editing, copyediting, proofs, cover design, sales catalogue, they need the book a year before for the sales team. Okay, it makes sense. Patience is part of the job.
Small question about style: should I keep Japanese honorifics like "-san" and "Obaachan" in the English, or translate them to "Grandma" and "Mr."? Thomas did not say yet.

I like your answer: decide one rule and be consistent, and for family words like Obaachan maybe translate to "Grandmother" because it is about the relationship, but keep names. I will propose this to Thomas.
Okay, I go back to work. Mochi is on the keyboard again, heated pad failed.
Hello. Today not work, life admin.

My landlord, Mr. Okada, sent a letter: rent goes up from next year, from 78,000 yen to 85,000. He is a nice old man, he apologised two times in the letter. The apartment is small, 1LDK, and I work from the living room, which is also bedroom when I fold my futon. I am thinking maybe it is time to move.

I am looking at Suita, near Esaka station. Cheaper than Tenma for more space, and I could have a 2LDK with one room only for work. But I like Tenma, the shopping street, my favourite izakaya, the old man at the tofu shop who knows Mochi's name. I don't know. Nothing decided.
Can you help me make a comparison? Commute doesn't matter so much because I work from home, but I go to Umeda maybe two times a week for meetings or co-working.
That is helpful. Esaka is only 10 minutes to Umeda on the Midosuji line. And more space for the same money. Hmm. But the tofu man. I will think more.
Different topic: tax. As a freelancer I do 確定申告 every year with blue form, 青色申告. This year I will receive money from a UK publisher. How does tax work for foreign income? Will the UK take tax first?

Ah, the UK-Japan tax treaty, and I should send a form so the UK publisher doesn't withhold tax, and then I declare it in Japan normally. I will ask Harbor Lane for this form when the contract comes. Thank you, I didn't know.
Also, my accountant friend says I should start "invoicing in yen" for foreign clients. Is that common? Or better in their currency?
I see, depends on who takes the exchange risk. For UK publisher, pounds is normal. Okay, I will not be difficult.

Unrelated, but I am curious: why do British people say "cheers" for thank you and for goodbye and for drinking? Thomas writes "cheers" at the end of every email and once wrote "cheers for the cheers" and I didn't understand.
Ha, "thanks for saying thanks". British humour, very dry. I like him more now.
Thank you, good night.

Hello! The Harbor Lane contract arrived, finally. I signed it today and sent it back. Now waiting for their side to countersign. I will upload it so you have the details. It is long so I copied the main parts as text.
Can you check if anything is strange? Especially the deadlines and the payment. I have never had a literary contract before.
Okay, so: fee per 1,000 words, paid in thirds, the deadlines, the credit on the cover, royalty after advance earns out. Nothing strange, you say it is a fair standard contract. I'm relieved.

The part about "house style: British English spelling" — I learned American spelling at school and in most of my commercial work. I need to be careful: colour, realise, travelling. Do you know a good way to set Word to British English for one document only?
Thank you. Done. The red lines everywhere now under my "color". It feels like being corrected by a strict teacher.
Also it says I will be credited on the cover. Thomas said in an email this is Harbor Lane's policy for all translations. I'm so happy about that. My name on the cover of a real book.
What is "moral right to be identified"? It's in clause 9.
Okay, so even if they change something, my name must be connected to my work, and I can object to bad treatment. Good.
I will start translating properly when they countersign. Thomas says "a few days". Fingers crossed.

Good news! Harbor Lane countersigned the contract. Thomas sent the PDF this morning with a very British email: "Delighted to say we're all signed and sealed; welcome aboard properly." So now the Kawabe book is officially my job. I started chapter 1 today at 6am, with coffee and Mochi on my feet instead of the keyboard (heated pad finally works).

But now I have a new worry. The novel uses a lot of Kishu dialect, 紀州弁, in the dialogue of the grandmother and the father. Some expressions I can guess, but some I really don't know if they are dialect or the author's own invention. The contract says questions to the author go through her agent, Ms. Fujimori at Tsubaki Literary Agency. I prepared a list of questions. Can you check my English is polite and clear? She reads English but I will also write in Japanese.

"Dear Ms. Fujimori,
Thank you for your support with the English translation of Shio no Kajuen. I have begun the translation and I would be very grateful if you could pass the following questions to Kawabe-sensei. I understand she is busy, so there is no rush, but answers before the end of October would help me very much to finish the first half on schedule.

1. Chapter 2, p. 31: The grandmother says 「ほんまにあんたはいっつもよう言わんわ」. I understand 'よう言わん' as 'I can't say it / I don't have the heart to say it', but in context it might be an expression of exasperated affection. Which is closer to the intended nuance?
2. Chapter 3, p. 48: The word 「あがら」 appears in the father's speech. I believe this is Kishu dialect for 'we/us'. Is it used here to emphasise the family as a group against outsiders, or is it simply his normal speech?
3. Chapter 4, p. 66: 「つれ」 — in Kishu dialect I believe this can mean 'friend' rather than 'companion/spouse'. Could you confirm?
4. Chapter 5, p. 79: The phrase 「みかんの木は塩を覚えとる」 ('the mikan trees remember the salt') — is this a local saying, or the author's own image? If it is a local saying, I would like to add a short note for English readers.
5. Chapter 7, p. 112: Haruka's mother uses standard Japanese while everyone else uses dialect. Is this intentional, to show she is from outside the region? I want to reflect this difference in the English.
6. General: Would Kawabe-sensei prefer that the dialect be rendered with a regional English flavour, or in neutral English with occasional rhythm differences? I have prepared a short sample of both approaches if she would like to see them.

With many thanks and best regards,
Yuki Tanabe"
Thank you, only small changes, good. I like your suggestion to attach the sample of both approaches directly instead of offering. Less back and forth.
For the sample, how would you render the grandmother's dialect in English without making her sound like a stereotype? I am afraid of making her sound like a cowboy or a pirate.

Yes, exactly, I don't want her to be Irish or Scottish by accident. Your idea: keep grammar mostly standard but use rhythm, shortened forms, a few old-fashioned words, and repetition. Like an old woman from the countryside anywhere. That feels right.
Okay, I sent it to Ms. Fujimori. Now I wait. Translators always wait.
Small Japanese question, because I'm tired and my brain is mixing: in English, "persimmon" — British people know this fruit? Or should I say "sharon fruit"?
Okay, "persimmon" is known enough, and "sharon fruit" is a specific variety marketing name. Persimmon it is.
Thank you. Good night, Mochi says goodnight too (she doesn't, she is asleep).
Hello! Another job came. This time a video game. I love games so I'm excited.

The company is Pinecone Games, a small indie studio in Stockholm. The game is called "Lantern Keeper", it's a cozy puzzle adventure about a girl who keeps the lighthouse lanterns lit on a group of islands. It was originally written in Japanese by the director, who is Japanese and lives in Sweden, and they need English localisation. The producer is Elin Berg. She is very organised, she sent me a spreadsheet with colour codes before we even talked about price.
The game release is planned for 26 February 2027 on Steam and Switch. So that's a different timeline from the book. Two big projects at the same time, scary but exciting.

The problem: they sent me the text strings in a spreadsheet but no access to the game build, no screenshots, no character sheet. I don't know who is speaking to whom, if the girl is talking to her grandfather or to a cat (there is a talking cat). In Japanese, speech style tells me a lot, but I need to see the context. Without it I can't really start.
How do I ask for the build politely but firmly? Game companies sometimes worry about leaks.
Good, I will mention I can sign an NDA, and that without context the quality will suffer and they will pay for more revision rounds later. Business argument, not emotional argument.
Can you explain the difference between localisation and translation? Elin used "localisation" every time and I want to sound professional when I talk to her.
Yes, localisation includes cultural adaptation, UI length limits, jokes, names, even changing references. In this game there is a joke about 「おでん」 that won't work in English. I will think about it.

Also another offer came yesterday, from a manga publisher in the US, Kitsune Comics. They want me to translate a slice-of-life manga series, 8 volumes. The pay is lower than literary but steady. I don't know if I can take it with the novel and the game. Maybe yes from next year? I haven't answered. I really don't know.

Can you help me think about capacity? Novel: about 92,000 words by end of January. Game: maybe 50,000 words, deadline in December. I translate about 2,500 to 3,000 polished words per day on literary, more on game text.
Hmm, so with both, I'm almost full until January, and manga would make me too busy. But maybe I can start manga in February. I will tell Kitsune I need time to think. Thank you.
Last question: what is "cozy game"? Elin keeps saying "cozy" with z. Is it American spelling?
Ah, "cosy" is British and "cozy" is American. Funny, the book is British spelling and the game is maybe American. I need to ask Elin which English they want.
Thank you, bye!

Hello. Some sad news, work-related. Thomas Pryce is leaving Harbor Lane! He got a job as editorial director at a bigger publisher. He told me personally by email, it was very kind. He said the book is in very good hands.

My new editor is Grace Odum. She has been at Harbor Lane for six years, she edited their Korean and Indonesian translations, so she knows translated fiction. Thomas introduced us by email yesterday and from now on I work with her. Thomas's last day is this Friday.

I'm a bit sad because Thomas found me and believed in me. But Grace's first email was very warm. She said she had read my sample and "the bus stop scene made me cry on the Tube". That's a good beginning.
Can you help me write a thank you email to Thomas? I want to say goodbye properly. Not too emotional, he is British.
Perfect. "Cheers for everything, including the cheers" — he will laugh. Thank you.
And a first email to Grace, introducing myself and my plan for the first half, and asking if she has any preferences for how I send queries? Not too long.
Good. Also I want to mention the honorifics decision I proposed to Thomas: names keep, family words become English. Thomas agreed, but I should confirm with Grace, new editor, new opinions maybe.
Sent. She replied within one hour: she agrees with the honorifics rule and she prefers queries as comments in the Word document. Very efficient.

Unrelated: I'm reading a book on translation theory, Lawrence Venuti, "The Translator's Invisibility". He talks about "domestication" and "foreignization". Can you explain simply? The book is very dense.

Okay, domestication = make it feel like it was written in English, smooth; foreignization = keep some strangeness so the reader feels it's from another culture. And Venuti says English translations domesticate too much and make translators invisible. Interesting, and a little political.
Where would you put my opening paragraphs? I think somewhere in the middle. I kept "mikan" not "tangerine".
Yes, I agree. A little foreignization with mikan, but the sentences are natural English. Okay. Thank you, my brain is full now.

Hello. I need to correct something I said before, sorry. The first half delivery for the novel is 15 November, not the 5th. I looked at the signed contract again and it says 15 November clearly. I told you and Thomas "5 November" from my memory. Grace also confirmed: 15 November for chapters 1 to 12.
Ten more days, I'm so relieved. That gives me time if Ms. Fujimori is slow with the answers.
Progress: I have finished chapters 1 to 4 in first draft. About 28,000 Japanese characters translated into maybe 26,000 English words. Hmm, is that right? I always confuse the conversion.

Ah, roughly, Japanese characters to English words, often around 0.5 to 0.7 English words per character depending on the text? So maybe it's less, 14,000 to 18,000 words. Let me check with Word count. ... 16,400 words. Okay, your estimate was right, my first number was crazy.

Can I ask about something difficult in chapter 4? There is a scene where the father says 「お前はもう、ここの人間とちゃうんや」 to Haruka. Literally "You are not a person from here anymore." It's very painful. My draft: "You're not one of us anymore." But it sounds like a movie. Ideas?

"You don't belong to this place now." Hmm, closer. Or "You're not from here anymore." The simple one is the most painful, I think. Simple and cruel. Like the father. Thank you, I'll use "You're not from here anymore."
Also, a question about numbers. In the book there are many measurements in Japanese units, like 反 for field area and 貫 for weight. Should I convert to metric? Imperial? Keep Japanese?

I like your idea: keep 反 only when it's important for the farmers' way of thinking, and convert to approximate English expressions in other places, like "a few acres" — but British readers use acres for land? Yes, for farmland, acres is still common. Okay.
Thank you. Back to chapter 5. The sea is calling, as Kawabe-sensei would say. Actually she would not say this, it is a cliché, she would hate it.
Hello! Two updates, both about life.

First, Aoi's wedding — I said 11 April before, but it's actually 18 April. Aoi changed it in the summer because the hall was available on the 18th with the garden room, and I didn't update my calendar. She was very angry that I had the wrong date in my head, "you are giving the SPEECH, onee-chan!". So: 18 April 2027, Kamogawa Garden Hall, Kyoto.

Second, I decided to move! I signed a contract for a 2LDK in Suita, near Esaka station. The move is on 28 November. One room will be my office, with a door, so Mochi cannot come to the keyboard (she will scream at the door, I know).

I'm sad to leave Tenma and the tofu man, but the space and the rent are better. The new place is managed by a company called Midori Housing, my contact is Ms. Ueno. So after the move, no more kind Mr. Okada, now a company with forms for everything. I will miss him.
Until the move, I'm still in my small Tenma apartment, working on the folding table.

Can you help me make a moving checklist for Japan? Address change at the ward office, electricity, gas, water, internet, post office forwarding, My Number card address, bank, and so on. And for a freelancer, anything special? Like my business registration address for tax?
Oh, the 開業届 address change for the tax office, I forgot. And my clients' invoices, I need to update my address for Harbor Lane and Pinecone. Good list, thank you.
Moving with a cat, any tips? Mochi hates the carrier more than anything in the world.

Leave the carrier open in the room for a week before with a blanket and treats, so it's not "the scary box". And on moving day, put her in the bathroom with the door closed before the movers come. Then the new apartment: one room first, then slowly the rest. Okay. Poor Mochi.
Internet: in Japan it can take 3–4 weeks to install fibre in a new apartment. I can't be without internet for work. What should I do?
Yes, I will apply now for the installation date, and buy a pocket Wi-Fi rental for the gap. Clever.
Thank you. Lots of things to do. I make a spreadsheet tonight.

Hello. Pinecone sent the official Statement of Work for Lantern Keeper. I'll upload it. Elin also answered my question: they want American English for the game, because most of their players are in North America. So: book in British English, game in American English. My spellchecker will have an identity crisis.
Can you read the SOW and tell me if something is unusual? Especially revision rounds and payment.
Okay, so per-word rate, max three revision rounds included, extra work hourly, payment net 30. And the string freeze date and final delivery. Nothing strange, you say. Good.

Hmm, but the SOW still doesn't say anything about access to the build. Elin said "we're working on it" in her email. Without the build I'm still guessing who speaks to whom. That is still the problem for the game.

Here is an example of why I need context. These are five strings from the spreadsheet, can you see the problem?

ID 1042: 「行ってくるね」
ID 1043: 「気をつけて」
ID 1044: 「…また？」
ID 1045: 「ニャー」
ID 1046: 「灯りを頼んだぞ」

Who says what? Is 1044 the cat being sarcastic or the grandfather? Is 1046 the grandfather to the girl, or the girl to the cat (that would be funny)?

Exactly. "Again?" could be annoyed, worried, or a joke, and the English would be very different. And 「頼んだぞ」 is masculine and a bit old-fashioned, so probably the grandfather, but the director told me the cat talks like an old samurai sometimes. I can't know without seeing.
I will send Elin these five strings as an example. Concrete examples convince producers better than complaints, I think.
Also, how do I handle character limits in UI? Some strings have a 24 character limit, and English is longer than Japanese.
Yes, abbreviations carefully, and ask if the font can be smaller for some menus, and keep a list of strings that don't fit to discuss with the team. Okay. Thank you.

YES. Elin sent the build! She gave me a Steam developer key and a short video of the main story with the director talking over it. Now I know who says what. 1044 was the cat. Sarcastic. 1046 was the grandfather. And the cat really does talk like an old samurai sometimes. I'm laughing alone in my apartment.
So the game is unblocked now. I played for two hours "for research". Very important research.

Another update from Elin: the director added a new side story with a fisherman and his daughter, so the word count goes up. The new count in the spreadsheet is 55,000 words instead of 48,000. She asked me if that's okay for the schedule.

Can you help me reply? I want to say yes, it's okay for the schedule, but I also need to mention the extra cost politely, following the SOW. I don't want to be the translator who surprises them with a big invoice later.
Good, I like "as per section 2.2 of the SOW" with the calculation, very clear, no emotion. Swedish people like clear, I think.

Now a creative problem. The cat's name in Japanese is 「おもち」, which is funny because my own cat is Mochi! (Coincidence, I promise.) In English, should the cat be "Omochi", "Mochi", or something translated like "Dumpling" or "Rice Cake"?

Hmm, "Mochi" is known to many English-speaking gamers already, short and cute, and keeping it gives a little Japanese flavor. "Rice Cake" sounds like a diet snack. Okay, I'll suggest "Mochi" to Elin. My Mochi will be famous.
And the samurai-style speech of the cat — in English how do I make an old-fashioned warrior voice without being too much like a bad movie?

Yes, formal grammar, "thou" no, but maybe "Hmph. You are late, young keeper." Short, proud sentences, some old words like "indeed" and "foolish". And the joke is when the cat says something very modern in the same voice. I love it.
Thank you! Back to "research" (playing).

Hello. The novel. Still no answer from Ms. Fujimori about the dialect questions. It's been almost three weeks. I sent a polite reminder. I can translate around the problem parts, but I need the answers before I deliver the first half on the 15th. So this is what is blocking the novel now.

Here is the passage from chapter 5 that I'm most worried about, with the "trees remember the salt" phrase. If it is a local saying, my translation should sound like a saying; if it is Kawabe-sensei's image, it should sound fresh. Here is my draft:

"Grandmother said the trees remembered the salt. She said it the way other people said it might rain, without looking up from her work, her hands moving through the leaves to find the fruit by touch. Haruka had heard it all her childhood and never asked what it meant. Now, standing in the lowest terrace with the wind coming straight off the water, she thought she understood. The trees nearest the sea were smaller than the others, their trunks bent landward, their leaves thicker and darker, as if they had grown a kind of skin. Their fruit was smaller too, but sweeter. Everyone said so. The Osaka buyers paid more for the mikan from the bottom terrace, though they never came to see the trees, and if they had come they would have seen only small, crooked, ugly trees and wondered why.

'They remember,' Grandmother said again, behind her. 'Every storm. Every typhoon. They keep it in here.' She knocked on a trunk with her knuckle, twice, as if knocking on a door. 'That's why they're sweet. Sweetness is what's left over.'

Haruka wanted to ask: left over from what? But Grandmother had already moved on to the next tree, and the question went where all her questions in this place seemed to go, out over the water, and didn't come back."

Thank you for saying it is beautiful, I am blushing. And yes, I agree "Sweetness is what's left over" works in both cases: as a saying or as her own philosophy. But if it is a known saying I want to add a short note in the translator's afterword. So I still need the answer.
How long is normal for an agent to reply in Japanese publishing? Am I impatient?

Okay, a few weeks is normal, especially if the author is writing a new book. Kawabe-sensei is writing her next novel, Ms. Fujimori said. I'll be patient but I'll mention the 15 November deadline gently in the reminder. Already did. Okay.
Different question. For the translator's afterword, how long is typical, and what should be in it? Grace said I can write one, about 1,000 words.
Good: a bit about the region, dialect choices, a few words I kept in Japanese and why, and something personal but short. Not a lecture. Okay.
Thank you. Now I take Mochi to the vet for her yearly check. She is screaming in the carrier already, and we have not left the apartment.

Hello. I wrote the first draft of my speech for Aoi's wedding. I timed it reading aloud: about 5 minutes. Here it is, mixed Japanese and English. Can you tell me what to cut and if the English part sounds natural?

「皆様、本日はお忙しい中、妹・葵と ダニエルさんの結婚披露宴にお越しいただき、誠にありがとうございます。新婦の姉の由紀と申します。」

"Good afternoon everyone. My name is Yuki, I am Aoi's older sister. For our guests from Hamburg: welcome to Japan, and welcome to our family. I'm going to speak in two languages today, so if you don't understand one part, please smile and nod. That's what I did for two years when I studied in London.

When Aoi was six years old, she decided she wanted to climb the persimmon tree in our grandparents' garden in Nara. Everyone said she was too small. She climbed it anyway, got stuck at the top, and refused to come down until our grandfather promised her she could keep every persimmon she could reach. She came down with eleven persimmons and a very proud face. I think that is Aoi: she climbs first and thinks later, and somehow it always works.

So of course she met Daniel at a climbing gym."

「ダニエルさんに初めて会った時、とても背が高くて、とても礼儀正しくて、日本語で一生懸命自己紹介してくれました。『はじめまして、ダニエルです。葵さんの…えーと…ボーイフレンドです』と。その『えーと』の間に、私はこの人はいい人だと思いました。」

Hello. A small personal project: I want to write some travel memories in English to practise more creative writing. Here's a short piece about a trip to Hokkaido two winters ago. Please correct only grammar and very unnatural phrases, I want to keep my voice:

"In February two years ago I went to Hokkaido alone. Everyone asked me why alone, as if travelling alone is a kind of illness. I wanted silence, and snow is the best silence in the world.

I took the night ferry from Maizuru to Otaru, because I am afraid of airplanes a little and because I wanted to arrive slowly. The ferry was almost empty. Truck drivers in the public bath, a family with a very small child who cried all night, and me. In the morning the sea was grey and flat like a sheet of metal, and then suddenly Otaru appeared, white and quiet, like someone had erased the colour from the town.

I stayed three days in a small inn near the canal. The owner was an old woman who spoke very fast in Hokkaido dialect and laughed at everything I said, even when I said nothing funny. She gave me hot milk every night before bed. I don't usually drink milk but I drank it every night because it felt like a ritual.

On the second day I walked to the end of the canal and sat on a bench covered in snow, which was a mistake for my trousers. I watched the snow fall into the water and disappear immediately. Thousands and thousands of snowflakes, each one perfect and unique, as the children's books say, disappearing in one second without any sound. I thought it was sad. Then I thought, no, it's not sad, the water is just made of all the snow that fell before. Nothing disappears, it only changes.

I think about that bench often. When I translate, sometimes I feel like the snowflakes, every Japanese word disappearing into the English. But maybe the English is made of them. Nothing disappears, it only changes.

On the last night the old woman gave me a small bag of dried squid for the ferry. I still don't know why dried squid. But I ate all of it."

Thank you! Very few corrections, I'm proud. "Which was a mistake for my trousers" stays, you said it's funny in a good way. And "like someone had erased the colour from the town", you suggested "drained", but I think "erased" is more my feeling. I keep "erased".

Here is a passage from chapter 8 where the mother speaks standard Japanese and the father speaks dialect, in the same scene. I made the difference visible in English, but I'm not sure if it's too subtle or too strong. Can you look?

"Her mother set the teapot down between them with the care of someone placing a stone on a grave. 'Your father thinks you should stay until the harvest is finished,' she said. 'I think you should decide for yourself.' She said it in the clean, careful Japanese of the city she had left thirty years ago, each word placed where it belonged, and Haruka understood that this, too, was a kind of argument.

From the doorway her father said, 'Harvest's not finished till it's finished.' He didn't come in. He stood with one hand on the frame, his boots still on, the way he always stood when he wanted to be part of a conversation without admitting it. 'Bottom terrace is still to do. And the Ishida boy's useless.'

'The Ishida boy is nineteen,' her mother said, without turning round.

'Nineteen's old enough to be useful.'

'You were useless at nineteen.'

'And look at me now.' He went back out. They heard the truck start, and stall, and start again.

Her mother poured the tea. 'He's frightened,' she said, very quietly, in a voice that was almost dialect, almost from here, as if for a moment the thirty years had worn through. 'He won't say it. But he is.'

Haruka looked at the steam rising from her cup and did not ask what he was frightened of. She thought she knew. She thought it was the same thing she was frightened of, which was that she would stay, and that she would not."

Good night.

Hello. My mother's 60th birthday is in December, it's 還暦 (kanreki), a big birthday in Japan. Aoi and I want to do something special but Aoi is busy with the wedding, so of course it's me. Here's what my mother wrote in our family LINE group when Aoi asked her what she wants:

"お母さんは何もいらないよ～😊 二人が元気でいてくれたらそれで十分。でもね、もし何かしてくれるなら、みんなで温泉に行きたいな。お父さんは仕事って言うと思うけど、たまには休ませないとね。あと赤いちゃんちゃんこは絶対イヤ！写真撮られるのイヤだから！笑 ダニエル君も来れたら嬉しいな。お母さん、ダニエル君にドイツのビールのこと聞きたいの。それと、お誕生日のケーキはいらないけど、あの梅田のお店のフルーツタルトは好き♡"

Summary for you: she says she needs nothing, but if we do something, she wants a family onsen trip, forcing my father to take a holiday. Absolutely NO red chanchanko (the traditional red vest for 60th birthday) because she hates photos. She wants Daniel to come so she can ask him about German beer. No birthday cake, but she likes the fruit tart from a shop in Umeda.
Ha, my mother. "I want nothing, here is a detailed list." Okay, so: onsen trip for the family, including Daniel, no red vest, fruit tart. Easy to plan, actually.

Can you suggest an onsen ryokan within 2 hours of Nara (where my parents live) that's good for a family of five, not too expensive, with private dining rooms? My father hates eating in big halls with strangers.
Arima is only an hour, and many ryokan have private dining rooms (個室食). And I must check the menu for buckwheat for me. I'll call and ask. Thank you.
Instead of the red chanchanko, is there something red but not embarrassing? Red is traditional for kanreki, I want a small touch.
A red scarf, or a red wallet, or red flowers. She likes gardening, maybe a red-flowered plant for her garden! A red camellia. 椿. She'll love it. And no photos, promise. Maybe one photo.
Date: her birthday is in mid-December, but I move on 28 November and the game final delivery is 18 December. Maybe the onsen trip after the 18th, like 20 December? Or should it be in January?
Yes, after the 18th is better for my stress, and it's still close to her birthday. I'll suggest 26–27 December to everyone. Daniel will be off work for Christmas probably.
Thank you. I'll send a message to the family group. My mother will say "you didn't need to" and then plan her outfit for three weeks.

Hello. Today a fun language question. Daniel's family are coming from Hamburg for the wedding, and I'm the family coordinator for the bride's side. I want to learn a few German phrases to welcome them. Can you teach me five useful ones with pronunciation in katakana?
Wonderful. 「ヘルツリッヒ・ヴィルコメン」 for "Herzlich willkommen" — warm welcome. I'll practise. And "Schön, Sie kennenzulernen" is long! シェーン・ズィー・ケネンツゥレルネン. Okay, I'll practise in the shower.
Daniel's brother Jonas is the coordinator for the groom's side. We'll work together on the day. I've only met him on video call. He seems nice, very funny, much louder than Daniel.
What are some cultural differences between Japanese and German wedding customs that I should prepare the German guests for? So nobody is surprised.

Oh, the money gift in an envelope (御祝儀) — Germans usually give presents or money but not in special envelopes, and the amount rules. And the hikidemono return gifts. And that Japanese receptions are very scheduled, with exact times, which Germans will like, ha. And no dancing usually. Okay, I'll make a one-page guide in English for them.

Can you draft that one-page guide? Friendly, practical, with small explanations, not a lecture. Include: money gift etiquette, what to wear (no white), photos not allowed during the ceremony, the reception schedule is tight, nearest station.
That's perfect. I'll ask Aoi to check it and then send to Jonas to share with the German guests.
Also, the German guests will probably want to see Kyoto. One day itinerary for the day after the wedding, with older people (Daniel's grandparents are 80), not too much walking?

Good: a taxi to Kinkaku-ji early, then a slow lunch, then a boat on the Hozu river? Hmm, the boat is 2 hours and a bit exciting for 80 year olds. Maybe Arashiyama by train and a short walk only. Okay, I'll make two options.
Thank you! Tack så mycket (wrong language, I know, I'm practising both).

Hello. Elin sent the updated Pinecone style guide, version 1.2. It's long and I want to make a short checklist from it that I can keep next to my screen. Here's the main part:

"PINECONE GAMES - LOCALIZATION STYLE GUIDE v1.2 (EN-US)
1. Voice and tone. Lantern Keeper is a cozy, gentle game about responsibility, community and small acts of care. The English should feel warm, light and slightly whimsical, never sarcastic toward the player (characters may be sarcastic toward each other). Avoid modern slang that will date quickly ('lit', 'vibe', 'slay'). Avoid profanity entirely; the strongest permitted expressions are 'darn', 'blast' and 'oh, barnacles' (the latter reserved for Captain Ume).
2. Player address. Use second person ('you') in tutorials and system messages. Use imperative mood for instructions ('Tap the lantern to light it.'). Never use 'the player' in in-game text.
3. Character voices. Hana (protagonist): curious, earnest, short sentences, occasional self-talk. Grandpa Tetsu: gruff, few words, warm underneath; avoids direct expressions of affection but shows them through actions and small praise. Mochi (cat): pompous, archaic-sounding but never using 'thee/thou'; delivers occasional modern phrases in the same lofty tone for comic effect. Captain Ume: loud, nautical expressions, mixed metaphors. Villagers: each has a one-line description in the character sheet; keep them distinct.
4. Names. Keep Japanese personal names (Hana, Tetsu, Ume). Place names: translate descriptive names ('Kazemachi' -> 'Windtown') unless listed as 'keep' in the glossary. The cat's name is 'Mochi' in all languages.
5. Capitalization. Title Case for item names, location names and achievement names. Sentence case for UI buttons, menu labels, dialogue and descriptions. Never use ALL CAPS except for single-word shouts in dialogue ('WAIT!').
6. Punctuation. Use the serial (Oxford) comma. Use the ellipsis character (…) rather than three periods. Use em dashes without spaces. Use straight quotes in the spreadsheet; the engine converts them.
7. Numbers. Spell out one to nine in dialogue; use numerals for 10 and above, and always in UI.
8. Length. Dialogue boxes: max 3 lines of 42 characters each. Tutorial popups: max 2 sentences. Item flavor text: max 140 characters. Button labels: max 14 characters.
9. Variables. Do not translate or alter variables in curly braces ({player_name}, {count}). Make sure sentences read naturally with plural and singular values; flag strings that need plural handling.
10. Cultural references. Japanese food and objects may remain (kotatsu, onigiri, mochi) if the context makes them understandable; add a light explanation in descriptions where needed. Replace puns and wordplay with English equivalents of similar spirit rather than translating literally.
11. Queries. Log questions in the 'Queries' tab of the spreadsheet with the string ID. The team answers within 2 working days (Stockholm time).
12. Glossary. The glossary (v1.2) is mandatory. Do not invent alternative translations for glossary terms. Suggest changes in the Queries tab."
Thank you, a short checklist is exactly what I needed. "Oh, barnacles" only for Captain Ume, I love that. And the serial comma, the novel's British style doesn't always use it, so again two worlds.
Wait, rule 7: numbers one to nine spelled out in dialogue. I used "3 lanterns" in some dialogue. I'll search and fix.

And rule 6: the ellipsis character "…". In Japanese text we use 「…」 too, so that's easy. But em dashes without spaces — in the novel, Harbor Lane uses spaced en dashes, I think. I need to check with Grace. Two style guides in my head. Help.

Okay, I'll make two small cards: a blue one for the novel (British, spaced en dash, no serial comma unless needed) and a green one for the game (American, closed em dash, serial comma). Colour coding. Or "color coding" on the green card. Ha.
Can you write both cards for me, max 8 lines each?
Perfect. Printed. Taped to the left and right of my monitor. Mochi already tried to eat the green one.
Thank you, this will save me from many small mistakes.

Hello. Weekend project: I want to learn to bake bread. Japanese shokupan, the soft milk bread. I found a recipe but I don't understand some steps. Here it is:

"Hokkaido Milk Bread (Shokupan) with Tangzhong
Tangzhong: 25 g bread flour, 125 ml milk. Whisk in a small saucepan over low heat, stirring constantly, until it thickens to a paste and you can see lines when you stir (about 65°C). Cool to room temperature, cover with plastic wrap touching the surface.
Dough: 350 g bread flour, 40 g sugar, 6 g salt, 7 g instant yeast, 1 egg (about 50 g), 120 ml warm milk, all of the tangzhong, 30 g unsalted butter (softened).
1. In a large bowl or stand mixer, combine flour, sugar, salt and yeast. Add egg, milk and tangzhong. Mix until a shaggy dough forms.
2. Knead for 10 minutes until smooth, then add butter a little at a time and knead for another 10-15 minutes until the dough passes the windowpane test (a small piece can be stretched thin enough to see light through without tearing).
3. Shape into a ball, place in a lightly oiled bowl, cover and let rise in a warm place until doubled, about 60-90 minutes.
4. Punch down, divide into 3 equal pieces. Roll each piece into an oval, fold the sides into the middle, then roll up into a log. Place the three logs side by side in a greased 1 lb loaf tin (about 21 x 11 cm).
5. Cover and let rise again until the dough reaches about 1 cm below the rim of the tin, 40-60 minutes.
6. Brush with egg wash or milk. Bake at 175°C for 30-35 minutes, until golden and the internal temperature reaches about 88-90°C. Tent with foil if browning too quickly.
7. Remove from the tin immediately and cool on a rack for at least 1 hour before slicing (it will be squashed if you cut it hot)."
Thank you. So tangzhong is like a pre-cooked flour paste that holds more water, that's why the bread is so soft and stays fresh. Like magic, but science.
I don't have a stand mixer. Can I knead by hand for 25 minutes? My arms are translator arms, not baker arms.
Ha, okay, the "slap and fold" method is faster and more fun. I'll try it. Mochi will watch from the counter and judge me.
Is there anything in this recipe I need to check for my buckwheat allergy? Bread flour is wheat, right?

Yes, bread flour is wheat, no buckwheat. But I should check the packaging for "may contain buckwheat" because some Japanese flour mills process soba flour on the same lines. Good point, I didn't think about that. I'll check the label.
My oven is a small microwave-oven combination. Will that work?
Okay, it works but I should preheat well, and maybe lower the temperature by 10 degrees and check earlier, because small ovens are hot near the top. And the 1 lb tin must fit. I'll measure tomorrow.
Thank you! If it works I'll take a slice to the tofu man as part of my goodbye. Bread and tofu, strange combination, but made with love.

Hello. For the future (maybe 2027), I want to pitch a short story collection to publishers. The author is Morioka Natsu, she writes very short, strange stories about everyday life in Osaka. Nobody has translated her yet. I translated one story as a sample. Can you read it and tell me if it would catch an English editor's attention? It's short:

"The Umbrella Office

On the third floor of a building near Tenma station, between a dentist and a company that sells industrial adhesives, there is an office that collects lost umbrellas. It has no sign. You find it only if you are looking for something else.

Mr. Kuroda has worked there for twenty-two years. Every morning at eight he receives the umbrellas the trains have left behind: the transparent ones, which are most of them, and the few others - a black one with a carved wooden handle, a child's yellow one with ducks, a man's folding umbrella still in its sleeve, as if its owner never believed it would rain. He writes each one in a ledger. Date. Line. Colour. Special features. Then he hangs it on one of the long metal rails that fill the room, row after row, so that walking between them is like walking through a forest that has decided to stand very still.

Almost nobody comes to collect their umbrella. A transparent umbrella costs five hundred yen; a train ticket to the office costs more. After three months the umbrellas are given to a recycling company, and the rails are filled again. Mr. Kuroda does not mind. He says the umbrellas are not really lost. They are only waiting, and waiting is not the same thing.

Once, ten years ago, a woman came for the black umbrella with the wooden handle. She was perhaps seventy. She said it had belonged to her husband, who had died the spring before, and that she had left it on the Keihan line by mistake, and that she had been looking for it for four months, at every station office, until someone told her about this place. Mr. Kuroda found it in the ledger, then on the rail, and brought it to her. She did not open it. She held it against her chest, the way you would hold a sleeping cat, and thanked him, and left.

Mr. Kuroda thinks about her sometimes, when it rains. He thinks that most things that are lost are not looked for, and that this is not sad, exactly, but that it makes the things that are looked for very important. He thinks he would like to be looked for like that umbrella, one day. Not by many people. By one person would be enough.

In the afternoon he eats his lunch at his desk, rice balls from the convenience store downstairs, and listens to the rain on the window, and counts, without meaning to, the people passing below who have forgotten their umbrellas and are walking quickly, heads down, through the wet streets of the city, toward whatever they are hurrying to, believing that they have lost nothing at all."
Thank you! You think the last sentence is the strongest, and the "forest that has decided to stand very still" image. I'm happy. Editors like a strong last line.
And you're right, "Special features" in the ledger is a little joke that I want to keep, it's like a product description for umbrellas.
Now the pitch letter to an editor. Should I write to Grace first, since I already work with Harbor Lane? Or is that unprofessional while I'm still working on the novel?

Okay, it's actually normal to mention it to your current editor, as long as I don't distract from the current project. Maybe after I deliver the first half, so she sees I'm reliable first. Smart timing.

Can you help me draft a short pitch? Not to send now, just to have ready. Include: who the author is, why she's special, the collection (14 stories, about 45,000 words in English), that rights are available as far as I know, and that I can send the sample.

Good. Short and clear. "Morioka writes about the overlooked corners of Osaka with the precision of a poet and the timing of a comedian" — a little bit marketing, but editors like a one-line hook. I'll keep it.
How do I check if the English rights are really available? I don't want to promise something false.

Contact her Japanese publisher's rights department, or her agent if she has one, and ask directly whether English rights are available and whether a sample translation can be shown to publishers. Okay, I'll do that in January when I have time to breathe.
Thank you. I feel excited about the future, even though the present is very busy.

Hello, a small English question. A friend sent me a poem she wrote in English for her grandmother's 90th birthday and asked me if the English is natural. I'm not a poetry expert, but can you look?

"Ninety winters on your hands,
ninety springs inside your laugh,
you taught me how to fold a crane
and how to cut an apple in half
so that the star inside shows through -
a secret only grandmas knew.
You never said the word for love,
you said, 'Have you eaten yet?'
and filled my bowl before I asked,
and that is how I won't forget:
not in words, but rice and tea,
the way you always cared for me."

Oh, it's lovely. The apple star and "Have you eaten yet?" — that's so true for Asian grandmothers. You say the only small thing is the rhythm in line 4, "and how to cut an apple in half" has one extra beat. Maybe "and cut an apple clean in half"? That keeps the rhyme with "laugh" and fixes the beat.
And "a secret only grandmas knew" — is "grandmas" too casual for a poem?
Okay, casual is fine because the whole poem is warm and simple. It fits. I'll tell her: change line 4 a little, everything else, don't touch. She'll be happy.
Thank you. Poetry is the hardest translation, even when it's already in English.

Oh, one more question about the poem. My friend wants to also make a Japanese version for her grandmother, who doesn't read English. She asked me to translate it, but keep it simple, not too literary, because her grandmother likes plain words. Should I keep the rhyme in Japanese? Japanese poetry doesn't usually rhyme.

Yes, I agree: no rhyme, but keep the rhythm with a 7-5 feeling where natural, and keep the images exactly: the crane, the apple star, 「ご飯食べた？」. The images are the poem, not the rhyme. I'll try tonight after work, it's a nice small gift to make.
Thank you. Good night, and Mochi says good night (she is asleep, as always).
Hello, one small question. In English, when do you write "Ms" and when "Ms."? I see both in emails from Grace and from Elin and I'm confused.

Ah, British English usually no full stop (Ms, Mr, Dr) and American English with a full stop (Ms., Mr., Dr.). So again British for the novel, American for the game. My two worlds even in the titles. Okay, I'll add it to my blue and green cards.
And "Mx"? I saw it in a form recently.
I see, a gender-neutral title. Good to know, I'll be careful to use what people prefer. Thank you!

Hello. Something is bothering me. A Japanese client, the Tokyo technical manual company, asked me if I can do "MTPE" — machine translation post-editing — for half my normal rate. They say the AI does most of the work. I want to understand the situation better before I answer. A colleague sent me this article, what do you think, is it fair?

"The Translator's Dilemma: Post-Editing and the Future of the Profession
Over the past few years, machine translation has improved dramatically, particularly for language pairs with large amounts of training data. For many types of commercial content - product descriptions, technical documentation, internal communications - machine output is now often usable as a first draft. As a result, many language service providers have shifted towards 'machine translation post-editing' (MTPE) workflows, in which a human translator reviews and corrects machine output instead of translating from scratch.
Proponents argue that MTPE increases productivity, reduces costs for clients and allows translators to handle larger volumes. Some studies report productivity gains of 30 to 50 percent for certain text types. Critics point out that these gains vary enormously depending on the content, the language pair and the quality of the machine output. For language pairs with very different structures, such as Japanese and English, machine output may contain subtle errors in meaning, register and coherence that are harder to detect than obvious mistakes, and post-editing can take almost as long as translation.
Translators also report that post-editing is cognitively different from translating. Rather than creating a text, they are constantly evaluating someone else's choices, which some describe as more tiring and less satisfying. There is also a risk of 'priming': exposure to the machine's wording can make translators accept awkward or inaccurate phrasing they would never have produced themselves.
Rates for MTPE are often set at 50 to 70 percent of standard translation rates, based on the assumption of higher productivity. Translators argue that rates should instead reflect the actual effort required, which can only be assessed by examining the specific content. Professional associations recommend that translators evaluate a sample of machine output before agreeing to an MTPE rate, and that clients and translators agree in advance on the expected quality level: 'light' post-editing (making the text understandable and accurate) is very different from 'full' post-editing (making it indistinguishable from human translation).
For literary translation, the consensus among practitioners remains that machine translation is of limited use, as the work depends on voice, rhythm, ambiguity and cultural nuance. However, publishers are watching developments closely, and some have experimented with machine-assisted workflows for genre fiction.
Ultimately, the profession is likely to divide: high-volume, low-visibility content will increasingly be handled by machine-plus-human workflows, while high-value content, including marketing, legal, medical and literary texts, will continue to require skilled human translators - who may also use machine tools as one resource among many."

So: ask for a sample of their machine output first, clarify light vs full post-editing, and set the rate based on real effort, not an automatic 50%. For technical manuals Japanese to English, the machine output is probably decent for simple parts and bad for complex warnings. Okay.
Can you help me write a reply to the client? Professional, open to trying, but I want to test a sample first.
Good. I like "I'm happy to explore this, and to make sure the quality stays where your customers expect it, I'd like to evaluate a 1,000-word sample first." Calm, not defensive.
Honestly, does this worry you for my future? Should I worry?
Thank you. Literary and games are the human-voice side, so I'm in a good place. And using tools for terminology and consistency is fine. I'll keep the technical client but not depend on it.
Okay, enough serious thinking. What's a good, simple dinner for a tired person? Fish, vegetables, rice — no buckwheat, and nothing that needs more than one pan.
Salmon and mushroom takikomi gohan in the rice cooker! Zero pans! Genius. Thank you.

Hello. Moving preparation. I'm throwing away things before the move. Osaka has strict garbage rules for big items, 粗大ごみ. Here's my list of things I want to get rid of, can you help me sort into: big garbage (needs reservation and sticker), normal garbage, recycling, or sell/give away?

- old folding table (my current desk!)
- futon (old, 7 years)
- small bookshelf, wood, 90 cm
- broken electric kettle
- 40 old paperback books in English and Japanese
- an old laptop (2016)
- winter coat I never wear
- cat tower that Mochi never used (she prefers boxes)
- printer that only prints in pink
- 6 empty wine bottles
- old curtains (the new apartment has different window sizes)
- a big plastic storage box, cracked
- desk lamp, works fine but ugly
- 3 pairs of shoes
- old phone, 2019
- frying pan, the coating is coming off

Thank you. So the laptop and phone are under the small appliance recycling law, I must use a special collection or the ward box, and delete data first. The printer is big garbage or small appliance depending on size. And books, the second-hand bookshop or the library donation. The cat tower, I can give away on Jimoty, maybe another cat will love it.
How do I safely delete data from the old laptop? It has old client files.
Okay, a full reset with drive wipe, or if it's very old just remove the drive and destroy it. I'll take out the drive, it's easier, and smash it with a hammer. Very satisfying, I think.
For the reservation of big garbage, how early should I book in Osaka? The move is the 28th of November.
At least two weeks before, especially at the end of the month when everyone moves. I'll book this week. Thank you.
The new apartment needs curtains. In Japan, curtain sizes are standard? I measured the windows: 100 x 178 cm and 200 x 135 cm.
Yes, those are common standard sizes, I can buy ready-made at Nitori. For the work room, blackout curtains so the morning sun doesn't hit the screen. Good idea.
I'll miss this tiny apartment a little. Seven years here. Mochi came here as a kitten. Okay, I'm not crying, you are crying.

Hello. I want to write a goodbye letter to the old man at the tofu shop in Tenma shopping street. He knows Mochi's name even though he has never met her, because I talk about her all the time. I wrote it in Japanese. Can you check the feeling is right? And maybe give me an English version for my blog someday:

「豆腐屋のおじさんへ
いつも美味しいお豆腐をありがとうございます。七年間、ほぼ毎週土曜日にお店に通わせていただきました。朝早く、まだ商店街が静かな時間に、湯気の向こうからおじさんが「おはようさん、今日はモチちゃん元気か？」と声をかけてくれるのが、私の一週間で一番好きな時間でした。
来月、吹田に引っ越すことになりました。仕事部屋が欲しくて決めたのですが、天満を離れるのは本当に寂しいです。特におじさんの絹ごしと厚揚げが食べられなくなるのが一番寂しいです。
吹田からでも、たまには電車に乗って買いに来ます。その時は、モチの写真を持ってきますね。
いつまでもお元気で。
由紀」

Thank you. You say the feeling is warm and natural, good. 「通わせていただきました」 maybe a little too formal for him, he speaks Osaka-ben with everyone, but it's a letter, so a little formal is okay. I'll keep it.

And the English version: "Every Saturday morning, while the shopping street was still quiet, you'd call out through the steam, 'Morning! How's Mochi doing?'" — I love "through the steam". That's exactly the picture.
Should I bring a small gift with the letter? What's appropriate?
A small box of sweets from somewhere he doesn't usually go, and the photo of Mochi printed! Yes, the photo is the real gift. He'll put it on the wall next to the calendar, I know him.
Also, my favourite izakaya in Tenma, "Kurumi", the master is also kind. Should I say goodbye there too? I feel silly, it's only 20 minutes by train, not another country.
You're right, I'll go one last time before the move, not as a goodbye but as "see you sometimes". No letter. Just eat and drink and say I'll come back.
And the new neighbourhood, Esaka, I don't know anything. How do I find "my places" in a new area?
Walk without a plan in the first weeks, go to the same café three times so they remember you, find the nearest bookshop and the best bakery. And check if there's a tofu shop! Okay, a mission.
Hello, quick update and then I work.
Still no answer from Ms. Fujimori, even after Grace's email. Grace says she'll call the agency next week, she has a Japanese-speaking colleague. So the novel is still waiting on the dialect answers.
And Kitsune: still undecided. I'll decide by the end of the month like I promised.

Game: 31,000 words done. Ahead of schedule. Elin sent the achievement icons, so now I can make the puns. One icon is a cat sleeping on a lantern. I named the achievement "Purr-manent Light". Too much?
Okay, you say puns are welcome per Elin's email and this one is visual and works with the icon. I keep it. Mochi approves (she is asleep).
Can you help me with one more: an achievement for lighting all the lanterns on the last island. Icon: a lighthouse at night with all windows lit. Japanese name 「すべての灯り」, "All the Lights".
"Every Light Burning" is beautiful but serious. "Lights, All of Them" is funny. "Keeper of Every Light" — oh, I like this, it connects to the title. Thank you.
Okay, back to work. Thank you for always being here, even at 6am.

HARBOR LANE PRESS LTD
14 Cloth Fair, London EC1A 7JQ, United Kingdom

TRANSLATION AGREEMENT (extract of principal terms)

Between: Harbor Lane Press Ltd ("the Publisher")
and: Yuki Tanabe, Osaka, Japan ("the Translator")

Work: SHIO NO KAJUEN by Kawabe Rin (original Japanese edition published by a Tokyo publisher), English title provisionally THE SALT ORCHARD ("the Work"). English-language translation rights licensed to the Publisher through Tsubaki Literary Agency, Tokyo.

1. COMMISSION. The Publisher commissions the Translator to translate the Work from Japanese into English, complete and without abridgement, in accordance with the Publisher's house style (British English spelling and punctuation).

2. DELIVERY.
2.1 The Translator shall deliver the translation of the first half of the Work (chapters 1 to 12 inclusive) by 15 November 2026.
2.2 The Translator shall deliver the complete translation by 31 January 2027.
2.3 The Translator shall respond to the editor's queries and review the copyedited text and proofs within the reasonable timescales set by the Publisher, normally not less than ten working days for each stage.

3. FEE.
3.1 The Publisher shall pay the Translator a fee of GBP 95 (ninety-five pounds sterling) per 1,000 words of the English translation as delivered and accepted. The length of the translation is estimated at 92,000 words, giving an estimated fee of GBP 8,740.
3.2 The fee shall be paid in three equal instalments based on the estimated fee: one third on signature of this Agreement by both parties; one third on delivery of the first half under clause 2.1; and the balance, adjusted to the final word count, on acceptance of the complete translation.

4. ROYALTY. Once the fee has been recouped, the Publisher shall pay the Translator a royalty of 1% of the Publisher's net receipts on all editions of the translation sold.

5. CREDIT. The Translator shall be credited by name on the front cover, the title page and in all publicity materials where the author is named.

6. QUERIES TO AUTHOR. Questions concerning the meaning of the original text shall be directed to the Author through the Author's agent, Tsubaki Literary Agency (contact: Ms. Fujimori Keiko). The Publisher will facilitate communication where necessary.

7. PUBLICATION. The Publisher intends to publish the translation within eighteen months of acceptance of the complete translation.

8. TAX. The Publisher will pay without deduction of UK tax upon receipt of a valid double taxation treaty form from the Translator.

9. MORAL RIGHTS. The Translator asserts the right to be identified as the translator of the Work.

10. COPYRIGHT. Copyright in the translation shall remain with the Translator, who grants the Publisher an exclusive licence for the full term of the Publisher's licence of the Work.

11. EDITING. The Publisher shall have the right to edit the translation for house style, clarity and length, but shall not make substantive changes to the meaning or tone without consulting the Translator. The Translator shall be sent the edited text, the copyedited text and one set of proofs for approval. Approval shall not be unreasonably withheld or delayed.

Project: LANTERN KEEPER - Japanese to English localisation
Pinecone contact: Elin Berg, Producer (elin.berg@pineconegames.se)
Accounts: invoices@pineconegames.se

1. SCOPE
1.1 Translation and localisation of all in-game text for Lantern Keeper from Japanese into English (United States), including dialogue, UI, item descriptions, tutorial text, achievements and store page copy.
1.2 Estimated volume: 48,000 source-equivalent English words, as counted in the localisation spreadsheet provided by Pinecone (version 0.9).
1.3 Target locale: en-US. American spelling and punctuation conventions shall be used throughout (e.g., "color", "cozy"). The Pinecone style guide (v1.2) takes precedence where it differs.

2. RATE AND FEES
2.1 Rate: USD 0.11 per word of the estimated volume, i.e. an estimated fee of USD 5,280.
2.2 Changes in volume: if the final word count exceeds the estimate by more than 5%, the additional words shall be billed at the same per-word rate, upon written confirmation by Pinecone (a "Change Order"). Reductions in volume will reduce the fee accordingly.
2.3 Revisions: the fee includes up to three (3) rounds of revisions requested by Pinecone after the initial delivery. Additional revision rounds, and any rework caused by changes to source text after the string freeze, shall be billed at USD 45 per hour.

3. SCHEDULE
3.1 String freeze (no further source text changes without a Change Order): 20 November 2026.
3.2 First full delivery of localised text: 4 December 2026.
3.3 Final delivery after revisions and LQA (linguistic quality assurance) feedback: 18 December 2026.
3.4 Planned commercial release (for information only; not a Contractor obligation): 26 February 2027, Steam and Nintendo Switch.

4. MATERIALS
4.1 Pinecone will provide the localisation spreadsheet, the Pinecone style guide, a glossary of key terms, and, where available, reference screenshots and/or access to development builds under the confidentiality terms of the Master Services Agreement.

5. PAYMENT
5.1 The Contractor shall invoice 50% of the estimated fee on first full delivery and the remaining balance (adjusted for any Change Orders) on final delivery.
5.2 Invoices are payable within thirty (30) days of receipt, in USD by international bank transfer. Pinecone bears its own bank charges.

5.3 Change Orders: a Change Order may be requested by either party by email and becomes binding when confirmed in writing by the Pinecone producer. Each Change Order shall state the additional word count, the resulting fee adjustment and any change to the schedule.

5A. QUALITY ASSURANCE
5A.1 After first full delivery, Pinecone's LQA testers will review the localised text in the running build and log issues in the shared bug tracker. Issues will be categorised as Critical (meaning error, missing text, broken variable), Major (wrong tone, inconsistent terminology, text overflow) or Minor (style preference).
5A.2 The Contractor shall fix Critical and Major issues attributable to the translation within the revision rounds described in clause 2.3. Minor issues will be addressed at the Contractor's discretion where time allows.
5A.3 Issues caused by source text changes after the string freeze, missing context that Pinecone failed to provide, or engine limitations (for example, font or line-break problems) are not counted as revision rounds.

6. CREDIT
6.1 The Contractor will be credited in the game's end credits as "English Localization: Yuki Tanabe".

7. CONFIDENTIALITY
7.1 All materials, including story content, character names and builds, are confidential until the public release, in accordance with the Master Services Agreement.

KAMOGAWA GARDEN HALL - WEDDING SCHEDULE NOTES (English version for family)
Couple: Aoi Tanabe & Daniel Weber
Date: Sunday, 18 April 2027
Planner: Hirano Mayumi (hirano@kamogawa-garden.jp, 075-555-0148). Please contact the planner, not the hall reception desk, for any questions.

THE DAY BEFORE - Saturday 17 April
- 15:00 Rehearsal in the Garden Chapel and the Garden Room (reception hall). Participants: couple, parents of both sides, Yuki Tanabe (sister of the bride, speech and family coordinator), MC, interpreter.
- 16:30 Final check of seating plan and gifts with the planner.

THE WEDDING DAY - Sunday 18 April
- 09:00 Family coordinators arrive (Yuki Tanabe for the bride's side; Mr. Jonas Weber, brother of the groom, for the groom's side).
- 09:30 Bride's hair, make-up and kimono dressing begins (bridal room, 2F).
- 11:30 Family photos in the garden (weather permitting; indoor alternative in the lobby).
- 12:30 Guests arrive; welcome drinks on the terrace.
- 13:00 Ceremony in the Garden Chapel (bilingual, Japanese and German/English, approx. 25 minutes).
- 13:45 Reception begins in the Garden Room (80 guests).
- 14:00 Welcome speech (groom's father), toast (bride's former teacher).
- 14:30 Meal service begins (French-Japanese course; see dietary notes).
- 15:15 Speech by the sister of the bride (Yuki Tanabe). Strictly maximum 3 minutes, including any translation, because of the timing of the kitchen service. Please send the final speech text to the planner by 31 March 2027 so that the MC and interpreter can prepare.
- 15:30 Bride's costume change (iro-uchikake to dress).
- 16:00 Cake cutting, games, video message from friends in Hamburg.
- 16:45 Letter from the bride to her parents; flower presentation.
- 17:15 Closing words (groom), guest send-off.
- 17:45 Family coordinators help guests from abroad with taxis to their hotels.

DIETARY NOTES
- Please inform the planner of all allergies by 15 March 2027.
- Already registered: Yuki Tanabe (buckwheat allergy - severe; kitchen will prepare a separate plate and avoid buckwheat in all shared items), Mrs. Weber (vegetarian).

DRESS CODE: Formal. Guests are kindly asked not to wear white. Kimono welcome.

PHOTOGRAPHY: Guests may take photos during the reception but not during the ceremony itself. The official photographer will share an online album within 6 weeks.

GIFTS: Return gifts (hikidemono) are arranged by the hall and will be placed at each seat. Monetary gifts may be handed in at the reception desk from 12:30.

INTERPRETER: A professional Japanese-German interpreter (Ms. Ishikawa) will attend the ceremony and the reception. She will interpret the welcome speech, the closing words and the letter from the bride. Family speeches that already include both languages (such as the speech by the sister of the bride) will not be interpreted again, but the interpreter will provide a short German summary card at each table of the groom's guests.

SEATING: The final seating plan must be confirmed by 1 April 2027. The head table will seat the couple only. Parents of both sides will be seated at the table nearest the entrance, according to Japanese custom. Guests from abroad will be seated together with at least one bilingual guest at each table where possible.

RAIN PLAN: If it rains, family photos will take place in the lobby and the welcome drinks will move from the terrace to the Garden Room foyer. The ceremony is indoors and will not be affected. The planner will decide the rain plan by 10:00 on the day.

ACCOMMODATION: A block of 12 rooms has been reserved at a partner hotel near Sanjo station for guests from abroad at a discounted rate, available until 18 March 2027. Please ask guests to book directly with the hotel quoting the reference "Tanabe-Weber".

TIMING REMINDER: The reception is scheduled to the minute because of the kitchen service. Speeches that run over will shorten the time for games and the video message. The MC has been asked to signal discreetly at 2 minutes 30 seconds.

TRANSPORT: The hall has no guest parking. The nearest station is Demachiyanagi (Keihan / Eizan line), 7 minutes on foot.
